lead: Only about 30 percent of the fuel energy reaches the crankshaft as work. Much of the rest soaks into the metal and must leave, or the piston rings lose their oil film and the liner scores. Cooling is the path that heat takes from the cylinder walls to the outside air. Air cooling hands that heat from fins straight to moving air; liquid cooling carries it in a coolant to a radiator. Motorcycles use the first; cars, tractors and most gensets the second.
prereq: You need: the engine components and the four-stroke cycle, and the meaning of indicated and brake power from engine testing and performance.

sections.h3: Why heat must leave the engine

blocks.text: Fuel energy does not all become work. In a typical diesel engine, of every 100 units of heat released by burning fuel, about 30 leave as brake power at the crankshaft, about 30 go out with the exhaust gas, about 30 pass into the coolant, and about 10 are lost to friction and radiation. The coolant share must be carried away all the time the engine runs.

Metal sets one limit: aluminium alloy pistons lose strength quickly when they run hot. Lubricating oil sets a tighter limit: above roughly 150 °C the oil at the piston rings oxidises, turns to varnish and coke, and its film breaks. A broken film means metal touching metal, and the liner scores. The oil system that keeps this film alive is in Lubrication systems and engine friction.

Temperatures inside a running engine are far from even. The burning gas briefly passes 2000 °C, yet the cylinder wall stays near 150 to 200 °C because coolant sits behind it. The exhaust valve head runs hottest, roughly 650 to 750 °C, so the jacket passages are packed closest round the exhaust port and valve seats. Uneven cooling is as harmful as no cooling: if one side of the head runs hotter, it expands more, and the head can warp or blow its gasket. Too much cooling also hurts: a cold engine vaporises petrol badly, wears faster and wastes fuel.

blocks.where: Q is the heat carried away per second in kW; ṁ is the coolant mass flow in kg/s; c is the specific heat of the coolant in kJ/kg·K (4.18 for water); ΔT is the temperature rise of the coolant in K.

sections.h3: Air cooling: fins, baffles and a blower

blocks.text: An air-cooled engine carries no coolant. Thin fins cast on the barrel and head add surface, so the same wall can hand its heat to a much larger area of moving air.

Fin spacing is a compromise. Fins packed close give more area on paper, but the air trapped between them stagnates and stops removing heat. Fins are kept thin to save weight and space, yet thick enough to conduct heat out to the tip; the real bottleneck is the air side, which removes heat far more slowly than the metal conducts it.

The air must be made to flow. On a motorcycle road speed does the job. A stationary pump set or a scooter with an enclosed engine has no useful road air, so a fan pushes air and sheet-metal cowls guide it between the fins instead of letting it slip around the outside.

Air cooling suits motorcycles, scooters, small pump sets and aircraft piston engines. It has no radiator, no pump and no coolant to freeze or leak, and it warms up fast. Its weakness is the small heat transfer coefficient of air, so the metal runs hotter and power per litre is limited.

sections.h3: Liquid cooling: jacket, radiator, pump, thermostat

blocks.text: A liquid-cooled engine wraps the hot parts in a jacket: a hollow space cast into the block and head, running close to the liner, the valve seats and the exhaust port. Coolant in the jacket picks up heat, a pump pushes it to the radiator, and air flowing over thin tubes and fins takes the heat out of it. Some syllabi call this indirect cooling, because the air never touches the hot metal.

The circuit has four parts. The water pump is a small belt-driven centrifugal pump. The radiator is the heat exchanger. The fan pulls air through it when the vehicle is slow or standing. The thermostat is a valve filled with wax: it stays shut while the engine is cold, so the engine warms up quickly, then opens at its set temperature and lets coolant through the radiator.

Liquid removes far more heat from a given area of metal than air does, so the jacket stays compact and all cylinders run at nearly the same temperature. The price is weight, cost, pump power and parts that can leak. Circulation by pump, by density difference, and under a pressure cap that raises the boiling point is covered in Thermosyphon, forced circulation and pressure cooling.

Below, a cooling loop: engine jacket, thermostat, radiator with fan, and pump. A box gives the coolant flow 1.12 kilograms per second.

examples.question: A genset engine burns 8 kg of diesel per hour. The calorific value of the diesel is 42 000 kJ/kg. Thirty percent of the fuel energy leaves through the coolant. The water may rise 6 K; c = 4.18 kJ/kg·K. Find (a) the fuel power, (b) the heat rate carried by the coolant, (c) the coolant mass flow in kg/s and in kg/min.
steps: Convert the fuel flow to kg/s: ṁf = 8 kg/h ÷ 3600 s/h = 2.222 × 10⁻³ kg/s.
Fuel power Pf = 2.222 × 10⁻³ kg/s × 42 000 kJ/kg = 93.33 kW.
Heat to coolant Q = 0.30 × 93.33 kW = 28.0 kW.
Rearrange Q = ṁ c ΔT for the flow: ṁ = Q ÷ (c ΔT) = 28.0 kW ÷ (4.18 kJ/kg·K × 6 K) = 28.0 ÷ 25.08 = 1.12 kg/s.
Convert to per minute: 1.12 kg/s × 60 s/min = 67 kg/min.
examples.answer: Fuel power is 93.3 kW, the coolant carries 28 kW, and the required coolant flow is about 1.12 kg/s, that is 67 kg per minute.

examples.question: A 150 cc air-cooled engine must reject 3.0 kW through its fins at full load, with a heat transfer coefficient of 50 W/m²·K, mean fin temperature 160 °C and air at 35 °C. (a) Find the fin area needed. (b) Without fins the barrel and head offer only 0.08 m² of surface; what surface temperature rise would that need? (c) The same engine works a pump set in a closed shed where the air is 55 °C. Find the mean fin temperature for the same 3.0 kW.
steps: Convection from the fins: Q = h A (T<sub>s</sub> − T<sub>air</sub>), where h is the heat transfer coefficient in W/m²·K, A the fin area in m² and T<sub>s</sub> the surface temperature.
(a) Temperature difference = 160 − 35 = 125 K. A = Q ÷ (h ΔT) = 3000 W ÷ (50 W/m²·K × 125 K) = 3000 ÷ 6250 = 0.48 m².

(b) With A = 0.08 m²: ΔT = Q ÷ (h A) = 3000 ÷ (50 × 0.08) = 3000 ÷ 4 = 750 K. The surface would have to sit about 750 K above the air, near 785 °C, which no aluminium head survives. The fins multiply the area six times (0.48 ÷ 0.08 = 6).
(c) Q, h and A are unchanged, so ΔT stays 125 K. Mean fin temperature = 55 + 125 = 180 °C, 20 K hotter than outdoors, and the oil at the rings moves closer to its limit.
examples.answer: (a) 0.48 m² of fin area; (b) a 750 K rise, which is impossible, so fins are essential; (c) the fins settle at about 180 °C in the 55 °C shed.

traps: Starting the coolant calculation from the brake power on the nameplate. The coolant takes a share of the fuel energy, so start from fuel flow times calorific value.
Calling the thermostat a temperature sensor. It is a wax-filled valve that opens and closes the coolant path; the fan and the gauge are separate.
Mixing units in Q = ṁ c ΔT. With c in kJ/kg·K the answer is in kW; using c = 4180 J/kg·K with kJ elsewhere gives a factor of 1000 error.
Saying the radiator cools the engine. The radiator cools the coolant; the jacket is what touches the hot metal.

quiz.q: Name the two families of engine cooling systems and give one application of each.
quiz.a: Air cooling (motorcycles, small gensets) and liquid cooling (cars, tractors). Some syllabi call the liquid type indirect cooling.

quiz.q: What is the job of the thermostat in a liquid cooling system?
quiz.a: It is a wax-filled valve that stays shut while the engine is cold so warm-up is quick, and opens at a set temperature to send coolant through the radiator.

quiz.q: Why are cooling fins spaced apart instead of being packed tightly together?
quiz.a: Air trapped in very narrow gaps becomes stagnant and stops carrying heat away. Spacing is chosen so fresh air keeps touching metal along the whole gap.

quiz.q: Why is overcooling harmful to an engine?
quiz.a: A cold engine vaporises fuel poorly, its oil stays thick so friction rises, and water from combustion condenses in the crankcase and forms acid and sludge. The aim is a target metal temperature, not the coldest engine.

quiz.q: A petrol engine burns 5 kg of fuel per hour with a calorific value of 44 000 kJ/kg. Twenty-eight percent of the fuel energy goes to the coolant. Find the fuel power and the heat rate to the coolant.
quiz.a: Fuel power = 5 × 44 000 ÷ 3600 = 61.11 kW. Coolant heat rate = 0.28 × 61.11 = 17.11 kW.

quiz.q: An air-cooled pump set works in a closed shed. Explain, using Q = h A ΔT, why its fins run hotter than outdoors.
quiz.a: Q, h and fin area A do not change, so ΔT = Q ÷ (hA) is fixed. Hotter air lifts the fin temperature by the same amount: 35 °C air gives 160 °C fins, 55 °C air gives 180 °C. Duct outside air to the cowl.

beyond: Modern engine thermal management treats cooling as a controlled system: electric pumps and electronically controlled thermostats hold metal temperature at a chosen value instead of letting it float. Battery packs and traction motors in electric vehicles use liquid cold plates built on the same jacket logic. Search terms: engine thermal management, split cooling, coolant control valve.
